utterances.text: It was not a private enterprise, nor was it the property of the municipality. It was so-called socially owned company. That's how it was called in the previous system in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did that mean that the municipality had to authorise the use to which it was put?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Municipal authorities were in charge of issuing various authorisations, probably also for catering businesses. If you wanted to open a catering facility, you had to obtain all kinds of approvals from the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The fire station, did that come under the control of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The football field, did that come under the control of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, under the control of the municipality? It was owned by the football club. It was not owned by the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you had no ability to direct to what use that football field was put?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the football field was a football field, and that was its purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was then, as you've admitted, turned into a massive prison camp, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the place where the people we were talking about were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These were prisoners, weren't they? People weren't allowed to leave, the Muslims who were incarcerated there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that these people were prisoners, that they had been arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And arrested for what?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's really hard to explain the situation which followed all these events. These people wanted to leave the municipality. If they were not given the opportunity to leave the municipality, they wanted to remain together. In the chaos that reigned, I cannot say that they were in captivity. I cannot say that they were free either. They did not have the freedom of movement to go wherever they wanted to. But at any rate, there was in group of people who wanted to leave the municipality and Bosnia and Herzegovina, but they wanted to stay together because of the fear that they felt. I cannot, therefore, say that there was a reason for their or some criminal offence for which they had been arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why I asked you the question. Arrested for what? They hadn't been arrested for anything. They were people, weren't they, who had been ordered out of their homes and villages or were fleeing from what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I'm able to answer your question. While it is true that they did not have freedom of movement and that one couldn't specify any crimes or criminal offences on the grounds of which they would have been arrested, but it is also true that they wanted to stick together. They requested to be allowed to remain together because they felt safer like that. And they wanted -- they requested the police that they be protected from the individuals and the groups that we talked about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you're saying the police placed them there for their own protection?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was also one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Muslims who were captured were taken to the fire station and held there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really not familiar with the details of what was going on at the fire station. This was completely outside my scope of activities, and it was not a piece of information that I would have been familiar with at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. You, as a member of the crisis staff, which I suggest was operating during this period, were familiar, weren't you, with the fact that people were being kept in the fire station?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, once again, this all happened around the 12th of May, the critical times, and I spent maximum of my time in Kostajnica. And it's possible that for a couple of days I was only in Kostajnica because of what was going on. So if we are talking about this particular period of time and the time that followed immediately after that, I really had no idea whatsoever as to what could have been happening there, if that is the period of time we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm suggesting this is the period between the 12th of May and the end of July when the municipality deported nearly all of its Muslims. Now, are you saying during that period of some month and a half you were unaware of people being held at the fire station?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, now I'm somewhat more clear. I thought you were referring to the period of 12th of May. Of course, later, I learned that some people were being held at the fire station, at the Una Hotel, and the football field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make any inquiries as to what these people were being kept - leave aside the football field for the moment - in the fire station for?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously we discussed the position of those people, the situation they found themselves in. I didn't inquire as to the reasons why they were being held there. But I requested that they be treated as humanely as possible, in a civilised manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you feel a need to make that request?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed it to be my obligation to draw the attention to the need to respect the rules of humanitarian law in view of everything that was happening at the time in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you feel it necessary to draw the attention of the police to the rules of humanitarian law? What was happening in Novi that made you feel it necessary?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously we had had information to the effect that certain individuals were treating those people in an inhumane, uncivilised manner. And to follow up on such information, I believe that we discussed and adopted very clear positions at the meeting of the municipal SDS, that those people should be treated humanely, in a civilised manner, that they should be given freedom of choice. Obviously, they couldn't -- they did not enjoy complete freedom. But at least, they could have been given a choice as to whether they wanted to stay or leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you did give such instructions, sir, or anyone else in your crisis staff or SDS, that was because, wasn't it, that you knew that people were being beaten up in these detention places and some of them dying?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous answer, I said that I had had information to the effect that certain individuals treated those people inhumanely. But I did not have any information concerning any death. Later, I heard that some of those people died. But at the time, I didn't know that. All I knew was that certain individuals treated them inhumanely, and that was the reason why we insisted on a humane and legal approach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certain individuals being police officers.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not know who these people were. I do not believe that professional police officers acted in that manner. I couldn't give you any name to that effect. But once again, I simply don't believe that professional police officers indulged in this type of behaviour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else had access to, first of all, the fire station?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not know who had access to the fire station. Believe me, at the time, I was not in a position to know the rules of the game. I didn't know who had the access to these facilities or who controlled them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the SJB? Because people were beaten and killed there, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm your allegation that someone was killed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the police --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I really cannot confirm that because I do believe that this did not happen within the police. I allow for the possibility, but once again, it is my opinion that such incidents did not happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that these incidents did happen. You can't say who did them. Was any investigation made into the people who were responsible for these unlawful killings, unlawful detention of these people?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really, I cannot tell you which cases were investigated and which cases were not. I did not work in the police. I'm not familiar with that. But it is my assumption that in connection of these events in Novi, the police applied the proper procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can't tell us. Who can? Who can tell us that information?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably the people who were in charge of that, who were in charge of relevant departments, military commanders for military issues, police commanders for police issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what was happening at the football field attracted the attention, didn't it, of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that was the case, that it was UNPROFOR that noticed a group of people at the stadium, that that was what attracted their attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. -- were you aware that Mr. Pasic and a member of the executive council, Mr. Rade, went to speak to officials from UNPROFOR on the 28th of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was Mr. Pasic who was in contact with UNPROFOR concerning these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the purpose was, wasn't it, to persuade UNPROFOR to let some 5.000 or so people, Muslims, leave the area?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the subject that they discussed, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And none of these people who Mr. Pasic was trying to persuade UNPROFOR to take were leaving because they wanted to, but because effectively, the actions of the Serbs were driving them out, that -- that's right, isn't it? That's right, sir, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're trying to lead me to an answer which I cannot answer with either yes or no. It is true that those people were fearful because of the events that were taking place. It is also true that they were the minority in the area where they lived, and they probably had their own reasons for leaving the area, for wanting to leave the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They posed absolutely no threat at all, did they, to the Serb domination of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Pasic tell you that he received a letter from officials, UN officials, explaining to him that what he and the Serb officials in Bosanski Novi were doing was a war crime?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me about that letter. All I know is that these people left with the assistance of the International Red Cross and UNPROFOR. This is completely new to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He kept entirely to himself the fact that he had received a letter telling him that this forced transfer or deportation of the Muslim population was a war crime. Never told you a word about that. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that we discussed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And part of the reason for the deportation of the Muslim population of Bosanski Novi was because of a decision made by the Autonomous Region of Krajina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What particular decision do you have in mind which would have been the reason for the departure of these people?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The one that was described as the "voluntary resettlement."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you got P227 here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that one?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look it up here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already told us --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you help us, Mr. Cunningham, the tab number, because we -- he was shown this document yesterday several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Tab number in his book is 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ten.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tab 10. Thank you, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually I don't -- I think it's later. It's that first -- I think it's a separate one, and I'm sorry I didn't pull it out. I'll find it, Your Honour, in the next break if it's necessary. But it's not in this one. It's a separate one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember -- leave aside the document because I think it's a later one. Do you remember a decision?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such specific decisions implying the necessity of those people to leave their homes, I don't remember them. I don't remember the particular one you're talking about. I don't remember a decision whereby those people would have been obliged to leave their homes. I really cannot recall any such decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just have a look for a moment, would you please, at Document P717, which is a report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, I've marked up the B/C/S copy because it's a long report dealing with a number of municipalities. So if we could have the English on the ELMO, though, please. It's page 8. And I'll hand the witness a marked B/C/S copy. Actually, I can tell you what page it is. In the B/C/S it's -- I can't, never mind. Just hand that to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was a report on a number -- to the Ministry of the Interior from the CSB dealing with a number of municipalities. If we look, please, at the part that's headed "reception centres in the Municipality of Bosanski Novi," there's no word about the football -- about the fire station or the police station or the Hotel Una, but the football field. You'll see in paragraph 3: "In the Mlakve stadium on the 11th of June 1992 members of the army from the area of the municipality quartered and provided security for 652 men of Muslim ethnicity fit for military service from the area of the Japra Valley whom the army had sent back from the railway station near Doboj, of whom 12 were younger than 18 and 27 older than 60." That was how they had come to be put into the football field, didn't they? They'd attempted to leave and been turned back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he explained this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it had nothing to do with the police keeping them there for their own security, either, according to this paragraph, because if you read the next paragraph: "The employees of the SJB in Bosanski Novi had no part at all in these activities."

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to apologise for not following completely because I was given a different page, not the one containing what you have just read out. I tried to follow and read at the same time. But clearly, my recollection is not very well as far as this time is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it was the police and not military units, so I accept I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry. No, it's my fault. I gave you the wrong part of the report?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction of the interpreter: The military and not the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's have a look, please. I think you've now got the right part of the report, the next paragraph: "The resettlement of citizens from the Municipality of Bosanski Novi. In the period from the beginning of the hostilities in the Municipality of Bosanski Novi until the 16th of August 1992 the resettlement of citizens has also occurred. As a result of frequent firing from the axis of the villages of Krslje and Rujiska --" It's that the one you've -- have you got the right one now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Usher, can you give them back to me. It doesn't help to mark if you hand over the wrong copies. Thank you. I'll tell you what. I think we'll give you the whole...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, do you see that? "As a result of frequent firing from these villages," those are Serb villages, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the first two are Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it describes about the first attempt to leave the municipality, 3.500. And then this: "Pursuant to the decision on the voluntary resettlement of citizens of the Government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the order of the Crisis Staff of the Municipality of Bosanski Novi on the criteria for voluntary resettlement, 5.680 people with proper documents left the municipality of Bosanski Novi on the 23rd of July 1992 and emigrated with the assistance of UNPROFOR and the High Commission..." et cetera. "Before we unregistered their official residences, these citizens gave statements before the competent municipal organs that their resettlement was voluntary, indicated the status of their immovable and movable property, and the men liable to military service obtained exemptions from military service because they were changing their place of residence." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember all the details, but it is true that these people left the area at the time, the area of the municipality, and it is also true that attempts were made for the whole thing to be carried out in a most humane and civilised manner to the extent it was possible, in view of the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Effectively, first of all -- not effectively, you, according to this report, you in Bosanski Novi, you in the crisis staff issued your decision as a result of a decision made by the Autonomous Region of Krajina, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember. But from this document, I don't think that the decisions are linked. The crisis staff decisions concerned the criteria for voluntary resettlement. The criteria on the basis of which one can conclude that the resettlement was voluntary. I cannot remember any other acts, any other documents to that effect. But this particular document doesn't show that these decisions were linked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. What does "pursuant to the decision on the voluntary resettlement of the Government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina..." What does "pursuant" mean in your perception?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really not in a position to explain this. I'm not able to give you an explanation. This was written by someone else. I don't know what the author of the text meant. The fact remains that we had to deal with the consequence of a large number of people wanting to leave the area. And on several occasions, as far as I know and I had been informed, there had been interventions on the part of the leadership of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the effect that we should prohibit these people from leaving the area. We were torn apart, so to speak, and it was difficult to work and act in a chaos of that kind. And I really cannot remember the specific contents of these two decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's have a look at another part of this report, please, which is the English -- well, it's the sort of separate report from Bosanski Novi itself, which is -- it's 011109856 at the top. And I'll give the witness, I hope, the...

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I point out an error in translation at line -- excuse me, page 57, line 57 [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 57, line 57 as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Transcript reads that "we should prohibit these people from leaving the area." I'm told by Mr. Vujic that the witness testified that he said that "we are prohibiting these people from leaving the area." So if that needs to be clarified with the witness, I wanted to bring that to the Court's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The transcript that I have here, which you should have as well, is "on several occasions as far as I know, and I had been informed, there had been interventions on the part of the leadership of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that we should prohibit these people from leaving the area." Now, you're saying that the witness said: "That we are prohibiting these people from leaving the area." Do you understand the point raised by Mr. Cunningham? Are you in a position to give us the right version, the corrected version? What did you actually say, Mr. Dejanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I understand your intervention, and it is an important one indeed. So -- could you please repeat to me once again what the transcript says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The transcript said that you had information at a certain point that the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had given instructions that you should prohibit these people from leaving the area. And then you continued: "We were torn apart so to speak and it was difficult to work in that kind of chaos." It's being suggested that you never said what I read out to you, but that you said that you had received instructions that you should prohibit these people from -- that you were prohibiting these people from leaving the area. Correct me if I'm wrong, Mr. Cunningham, but I'm confused as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'll defer to the witness because he's answered. I'll defer to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a significant difference. I don't think that I made a mistake. My words were probably misinterpreted. We were called upon by the leadership of Republika Srpska who told us that there had been complaints to the effect that we were not allowing the complaints made by the Muslims population, that the authorities in the municipality were not allowing them to leave, to go where they wanted to go. So that was the kind of intervention that they had, that we should not prohibit the people from leaving the area and going where they wanted to go. On the other hand, speaking of a decision like that, a mass departure of population from the area of the municipality obviously was not a good thing. So these are the two extremes, the two extreme points that I'm talking about, that I was talking about when I said that we were torn apart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dejanovic and thank you, Mr. Cunningham. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have slight problems at the moment. I know where it is in English. I thought I'd marked it, but I'm not sure I have. It's -- if we can have on the ELMO, please -- can you give me the report you've got there in English. Yes, that's what I want on the ELMO. And I'd like to see if I can find the B/C/S. It's possibly page B0032543, in B/C/S. Yes, here it is. Or is it? No, 43, sorry. No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a further part of the report specifically from Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] This is Sanski Most. This is Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Can I -- I know that you read and speak English, so can you look at what it says on the ELMO, and if there's any problem we'll find the B/C/S for you. "Pursuant to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Ministry of Defence decision, the decision of the Government of the Autonomous Region" and so on, "the confiscation of illegally acquired weapons." It sets out the background, which we've already dealt with. Then the attack alleged on a military police patrol in the village of Blagaj Rijeka. And we've found the B/C/S now, so you can have that, please. And then this: "As a result, a series of combat operations were directed against areas and villages with a majority Muslim population. Thus, on the 24th of May 1992, the entire population of the Japra Valley villages was put up in the central part of Blagaj Japra. After the burial of a member of the military police who had been killed during an attack on Prijedor, combat operations took place in the Prekosanje suburb." Is that the suburb of the town of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's a part of Bosanski Novi. Bosanski Novi itself is not very large, but it is a part of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "All the combat operations mentioned above were carried out by armed, uniformed men who were either self-organised or members of the Territorial Defence or JNA combat units..." Now, I asked you - I don't know how long ago now - whether you were aware that the JNA had taken part in an attack - I say the JNA, the VRS as it was by then - on the Bosanski Novi town.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of it. And I think that the JNA as an organisation did not take part in it. This is not an appropriate document. I see from the English translation that it says here "members of the JNA," so you can say that members, some members did do that. But I don't think that there were any planned operations targeting those civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not the right document. This is the wrong document. It's not the document that you're talking about. This is a report about the reception centres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Try that. I think I may have actually highlighted the right part. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that should be it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, that says, doesn't it, if you look at the B/C/S, "members of the Territorial Defence or JNA combat units"?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here: Self-organised or members of the TO or of combat units, and it also says here that members of the public security station did not take part in it. I still maintain that as far as I know, there were no planned operations on the part of the JNA, but it is a fact that members of these armed forces and, as it says here, "self-organised persons," committed what they had committed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move to a further part of this report. I'll give you that. That is marked. And we need to -- the English, it's 01109860. Do you see there, the next day, this deals with the refugees again from the Blagaj Japra: "The next day, the 10th of June 1992, 652 men fit for work were taken off the convoys in the Doboj area, returned to the Bosanski Novi Municipality where on instructions from the crisis staff, they were put up at the Mlakve collection centre." Do you agree that you gave instructions about that, you, the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the instructions, the specific instructions. I described yesterday the events pertaining to these men, and finally they were accommodated in the Mlakve stadium. I don't remember the crisis staff having discussed this. And let me reiterate, I don't mean to defend myself or to explain why I don't remember. I have to say that these were chaotic days, and I spent most of my time in Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you say, sir. And may I suggest to you that that's simply untrue. You were the head of the SDK in Bosanski Novi; you were a member of the crisis staff. I suggest to you that where you were was in Bosanski Novi itself.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not deny the fact that I was the chairman of the municipal board and that I worked at the SDK, but I have to stress that in the critical period, in the several days, I focussed all my attention to the events in Kostajnica. I do not deny that such an instruction may have been given, but I myself cannot remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But nothing was happening in Kostajnica. Why would you spend, as you explain, these critical days in Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was making efforts to prevent things from happening there. That is why I spent my time there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And finally, on that same page, we see yet again, and this time the word used is "proceeding" in English "from a decision on the voluntary moving out of citizens issued by the Government of the AR Krajina." Is that the word in your language?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I require some assistance here. Where is this passage that you've just read to me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two paragraphs further down, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it. Can you now please repeat your question, because as you were asking it, I wasn't following.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The word there, was it the same word way was used in the earlier one, which is translated in English as "pursuant" or is it a different word which is now translated in English as "proceeding," which perhaps makes it clearer?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Proceeding from."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's quite clear, isn't it, that the author of this report is firmly of the view that everything that was done in respect of that came about as a result of the decision made by the Krajina Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is that he's referring to the decision as a source, but I don't know why the author of this report is doing it. My assumption is that, as I have just said, that this was because of the chaos that reigned and because we were torn between the two extremes that I spoke about. And that is why when reports were drafted, documents that were available were used as reference. But I really didn't -- cannot say what the author of the report wanted to say -- what he meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was written, wasn't it, by your friend, the police chief, Mr. Kutlija?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We'll give you the last page. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 10. Ljubomir Kutlija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was a member of the crisis staff, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By virtue of his position, I think that he was supposed to attend the sessions of the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, he was on the crisis staff, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to a decision of the Republika Srpska Government, he was on the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was in a position to know what orders had been issued by the crisis staff and what the source of those orders was.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And this was an order dressed up -- euphemistically called "voluntary resettlement" which was an order to ethnically cleanse, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with this statement. This was an order about the criteria for voluntary resettlement or moving out. I don't remember what the criteria were, what one had to do for the moving out of these citizens to be carried out in as civilised and humane manner as possible. I believe that the criteria had to do with this, and not with the fact that they would be forced to move or that they had to move out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one thing before we look at the actual results. You told us yesterday that as far as you were concerned, and you referred to it again today, that you were keeping the peace in Bosanska Kostajnica and that - here we are - you were very successful in keeping the peace, that there were no victims, murdered people, you defined it as. It's on page 45. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please let me clarify. When I say "very successful," I mean to the best that could be achieved in the given circumstances. And let me just explain what the overall situation was like. I want to stress once again that this was something that I did as much as I could, to the best of my abilities given the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But all I want to put to you is you're not suggesting that Muslims weren't murdered, are you, in Bosanska Kostajnica? Are you suggesting that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period 1992, for example?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period, a very short period that had to do with the confiscation of weapons. But there were victims in Bosanska Kostajnica throughout the war. I don't remember when exactly. But I'm now talking about the period around the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you said that you kept the peace, there were no killings, you were referring only to the limited period of disarmament around the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I was referring to that period when I said that there were no killings, that nobody was murdered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, finally, I would like you to look, please, sir, at the Exhibit P60. Now, can you turn to -- this is the census document. Can you turn to Bosanski Novi, please, which is on the second page of the actual listing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Novi Grad, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. It's not called Novi Grad. It's called Bosanski Novi. It changed it's name sometime in 1993, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've found it. Page 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991, when the census was taken, there were -- sorry, just a minute -- 25.000 Serbs, just over, and 14.000 Muslims. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, have a look, please, at Exhibit P56. Could you turn, please, in that -- there it's called Novi Grad, because it's 1993. This is a report done by the Banja Luka CSB. It's on the second page of the English. First page, I suppose. "Moved out, Muslims, 13.000; Croats, 40.000."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 40, sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Serbs, no data. Moved out, none. And 3.400 moved in. 1.000 Muslims left in the municipality by May 1993. Do you accept that's a fairly accurate figure?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot discuss these figures. I don't know. The values can be approximate, but I do not know whether the figures are accurate. I don't know what they're based on. However, it is obviously, and I'm not denying it, that the majority of Muslims had moved out of the municipality of Bosanski Novi in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, not in the course of the war; in the course of less than a year effectively. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot confirm the data here because I'm not familiar with them. I don't know on the basis of what the Security Services Centre produced these figures. But I do not deny the fact that people had moved out from the area, that there had been people who moved out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Their mosques -- the mosques had all been destroyed, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The houses were either -- their houses were either burnt or occupied by Serbs. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is mostly true. I have to note that we had a large number of refugees. In most cases, the refugees were put in those houses, not the local population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Their cattle had been looted; their houses had been looted. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in essence, this was one of the most successfully ethnically cleansed areas in the whole of the Krajina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I can seek assistance here, but I have this feeling that things are being put to me which are not fair. I do not believe that there was the intention to carry out the ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say it wasn't intended --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Dejanovic, I will only stop Ms. Korner when indeed I agree with you that the question is unfair. But I don't think that the question that she put to you was unfair. I mean, it's a question which you can answer. And in your own way, you have answered it. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask, do I have to seek your intervention, or will you intervene on your own discretion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will not interfere with the questions put until or unless we come to the conclusion that that question shouldn't be put. But it doesn't mean to say that if a question has been put and we haven't interfered that you have a duty to answer that question if you feel that that question can expose you to criminal proceedings. I am saying this to protect you. In other words, our duty here is to protect each and every witness that comes forward. No witness can be forced to answer questions which can be incriminatory in their own nature unless there is reason for us to give the direction nonetheless. And if we do oblige you to answer a question which could be incriminatory if answered, then whatever you say cannot be made use of in any proceedings outside this Tribunal. So I'm making this clear to you. But I will not stop Ms. Korner or anyone else for that matter from putting questions to you which may be very uncomfortable to answer. But uncomfortable is one thing. Answering them and exposing yourself to criminal proceedings here or elsewhere is another matter. So if at any moment you feel you may find yourself in that awkward position, please do look up to us, ask for our intervention, and we will decide how far and to what extent to protect you. But we are here to protect you as a witness. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And effectively, that ethnic cleansing took place directly upon the decisions, starting with the level of the republic, passed down through the Krajina, decisions designed to separate the Serbs from the other nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, the war is a very serious thing, and especially for a group of people who are in the minority. The fear that the minority felt probably caused them to want to leave the area. The same thing happened in the areas where Serbs were in the minority. To my mind, these were the reasons that prompted so many Muslims to leave the municipality in the course of the war. In the areas where we tried to achieve a calming of the situation, a larger number of Muslims remained in the areas where they lived. This is all I can say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the moment, I'm just asking you this: Do you now accept, and you have been reminded of all the documents and all the decisions, that what you did in Bosanski Novi was as a direct result of the instructions, the decisions, the orders which came from the republic level and from the Autonomous Region of Krajina level?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the form of the question because it calls on him to answer about two distinct entities, the republic level, and the ARK. So it's a compound question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, he can take them separately. Please take them separately. And if you need Ms. Korner to repeat the question, we'll have her read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: With respect, the question is that the orders start at the top and are channelled through the mid-level. It's not a compound question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I still renew my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the way it is on the -- it shows on the transcript, well, would justify the comment made by Mr. Cunningham because -- the previous question had hinted that, or suggested that, but this one didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the moment, I'm asking you this: Do you accept and you have been reminded of all the documents, that what you did in Bosanski Novi was as a direct result of the instructions, decisions, the orders which came from the republic level and from the Autonomous Region of Krajina level? So they are taken -- anyway, let's stop here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have an answer to the question? It's my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Dejanovic, can you provide us with an answer now very shortly so we can have the break on time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that everything that happened was the consequence of the general crisis, general state of war, and the feeling of insecurity among the minorities, regardless of who the minorities were, living in an environment with a majority from another ethnic group. And I think that this gave rise to the consequences you have just described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was not the question. We'll take it up after the break. The question was, and please think about it during the next 25 minutes. The question that was put to you is the suggestion that what you - that means the crisis staff in Bosanski Novi - did was the direct result of instructions, decisions and orders that came from higher up. And higher up is meant republic level and the Autonomous Region of Krajina. So think about it and give us an answer as we reconvene. Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, but I'm informed by Mr. Vujic that he said that it was not the consequences of the order, and that didn't get translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't have it in my transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Nor do I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you actually answer that question and say that you never acted upon the instructions, decisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of my previous answer, I said this was not the consequence, not that we never acted in accordance with them, but that this was not the consequence of the orders. In my previous answer, I tried to explain that this was the consequence of the general situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We'll have a break of 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, again, once more, Mr. Cunningham, require how much time? Still in the 5-minute region?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Probably closer to 7 or 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Cunningham:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end -- at the very end of the business day yesterday, Ms. Korner asked you who you were working for during this time period, and you told us that you were work for the SDK. How many employees at that time did you have working with you at the SDK?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were about 10, between 10 and 14.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many non-Serbs were working with you at the SDK?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two ladies who were non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they continue to work with you throughout the period of May and June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period and later, yes, they continued. I don't know what happened after I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you leave the SDK?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, I believe it was. In March I was elected to a different position. And later, in 1994, I returned briefly to the SDK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to change topics. Ms. Korner showed you an exhibit. It was P186 which was a document from the ARK Crisis Staff dealing with per capita donations of 30 dinars to the ARK. Do you remember that document?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I think it is a document of the executive council of the municipality, not the crisis staff, if my memory serves me right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at the documents which are P186 and P2539. If we could look at P186 first.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the document that speaks about the distribution of... Is this P186?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reason I can't answer is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 186 should be the decision or the order of the municipal executive committee of the Bosanski Novi Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that document indicates, am I correct, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. That's P2539. 186 is the communication from the Autonomous Region of Krajina to the presidents of the municipal assemblies supposedly of the municipalities that are mentioned in the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, 2539 is the document that -- P2539 should be a document that is a Novi document. Do you have that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it's 2547.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I apologise. I apologise, that was my mistake. Do you have that document, sir? I'd like for you to look at 2547.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm think I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's my fault. It's 2539. I'm sorry, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you for restoring my sanity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's start from the top. I wanted you to look at P186 which is a document from the crisis staff sent out to the municipalities. And I think you've looked at that document. Am I correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I understand which document you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now the other document I want you to look at is 2539, which is a Novi document, and I believe that that -- this is -- tell us what this document says. I don't want you to tell us the whole thing, but I want you to read the relevant portion about -- I think there's an order or something in there. So read the relevant portion that deals with the money.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. It is stated here that the executive council of the Bosanski Novi Municipality hereby orders the secretariat for administration, that is, to a lower-level body, that for the purposes of financing the institutions of the Autonomous Region of Krajina a specified amount should be deposited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you know whether that order was ever acted upon; that is, whether the money was ever actually transferred to the ARK?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. I'd like for you to now in your book go to tab number 10. Tab number 10 is Prosecutor's Exhibit 227, which is the ARK -- Gazette of the ARK. I want you to read to yourself the introduction of that document where it says: "Pursuant to the decision..." Just read silently to yourself down to where it says "decision."

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, are you referring to the first decision in the binder?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The very first decision, the one that's marked number 1.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read the introduction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, looking down at paragraph number 5 where it deals with paramilitary formations and the illegal possession of weapons and ammunition, where did the instructions with regard to disarmament originate? Did they originate from the ARK or did they originate from a decision of the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clear from the preamble of the decision, from the introductory part of the decision that the decision maker is referring to a decision of the Ministry of Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Hercegovina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we didn't get the number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. I'm done with that document. I want to ask you about something you said earlier today. At page 41, line 13 of your testimony today, you talked about how municipalities had an obligation to provide logistics or logistical support to the military. Could you please explain to the Chamber what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the food, supplying the military with the basic necessities. The supplying of the military at the time was not a quality one. I'm now referring to a longer period of time as to what the obligations of the civil authorities were. First of all, food supplies, very often provisions of fuel. That's all I can think of at the moment. That kind of supplies or provisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the supplying of the food and the fuel, did that in turn allow the civilian authorities to issue binding commands to the military?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you in your book to turn to tab number 9. Tab number 9 contains Prosecutor's Exhibit 157, which is an excerpt from the work of the municipal crisis staffs of the Serbian People. This is the document attributed to Prime Minister Dzeric, 26 April 1992. On the second page, please look at paragraph 14. This is something you talked about with Ms. Korner earlier today. She was talking to you about paragraph 14 where it says: "The submission of weekly reports to regional and state organisations." Were you aware, actually aware of any reports that were submitted by the Novi Crisis Staff to the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any specific reports. I can only make assumptions in this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Final question has to deal whereby hopefully my final question has to deal with following up on what Mr. President asked you about the supreme command of the military, the supreme command in time of war. In a time of war, who would be the supreme command, if you know? I know you're certainly not a military expert, but I believe you did your compulsory JNA service. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right, yes. I served -- I'm not an expert for military or constitutional matters, but I believe I answered the previous question. It was always the presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm told that there might have been a nontranslation, so I'm going to go back and try to clear up a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please do, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This deals with tab number 10, decision number 1. I asked you based on your review of this document, with respect to paragraph 5, where did the decision with regard to disarmament originate? Did it originate within the Ministry of Defence or within the ARK?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read out what it says clearly. "Pursuant to a decision issued by the ministry of the National Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina" followed by the number and the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And that's all the questions I have. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was one matter. During our searches, a document came to light which had not previously been disclosed to the Defence. And so we gave it to Mr. Cunningham after the last break. I can tell you, Your Honours -- can I show Your Honours a copy. I was going to simply apply to tender it after the witness had left. But it occurs to me that we ought to ask, if Your Honours agree and Mr. Cunningham doesn't object, to ask the witness whether he's familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see what it's all about. Has everybody had the chance to read it? What's your position on this, Mr. Cunningham? Two points: One is the tendering the document as an exhibit; second, putting the document to the witness, asking him whether he's aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I wish it would have been tendered earlier, and I understand sometimes it happens when documents are not discovered as soon as they should be. Understanding the Rules of Evidence in this Court and the discretion that's left to the Chamber, and also recognising that we have provided documents at a late date, I don't think it would be equitable for me to object on the basis of timeliness of the disclosure. With respect to questions to be put to the witness with respect to the document, I would leave that to the discretion of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm not asking to reopen my cross-examination, simply whether he's able to -- whether he's familiar with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, the document is being accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And is being tendered as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's P -- Exhibit 2714.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And usher, could I kindly --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Here's a copy for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And Mr. Dejanovic, just have a look at that document which purports to have been signed for and on behalf of Radomir Pasic dated 8 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you can give me a moment, Your Honour, please. It's not really legible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Very simple question: Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be perfectly frank, no, I have not seen this document. I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a series of public communiques, public addresses, I accept the possibility of the existence of such a document. It was only part of a range of such interventions. But I never saw this document, and I never dealt with it specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Judge Taya is drawing my attention to ask for a clarification from you. The third paragraph, third paragraph says: "Since members of the Serbian army have been engaged in these duties day and night, and due to their" -- what's the next word? Is it fatigue? Desperation? What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fatigue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fatigue. Okay. And is there the word "desperation"? Can you continue reading, if you can decipher the letters? I know it's difficult, Mr. Dejanovic. I'm not asking the impossible from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe though I cannot say with certainty that we are talking about bitterness here, not deception. I'm not sure that this is the word. The interpreters will confirm. There is a difference between bitterness and desperation. I think that here we're talking about bitterness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the interpreters do not have the text, so we're not aware of the exact wording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, and my apologies to the interpreters for putting you in this position. I think we can leave it at that. Now, we have some questions from the Bench. We're going to start with Judge Janu. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Mr. Dejanovic, did you really believe at the summer and -- spring and summer 1992 that the resettlement of the citizens was voluntary?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that throughout my testimony I never said that it was a voluntary resettlement. I think I even emphasised that there could have been no voluntary resettlement considering the circumstances in which these people lived. I said on a couple of occasions that we did our best for this to be carried out in a most humane and civilised manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And in your opinion, was the Serbian population in comparison with Muslim, Bosniak population in a different condition?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the fact that Serbs constituted majority, and Bosniaks minority in the area, and also in view of the fact that there was already a war going on, obviously Serbs were in a better position, so to speak, considering the circumstances. So they were not in the same situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So you explain the fact that a number of Muslims who left your municipality and other municipalities in Bosnia is much higher than Serb just with this feeling being minority or majority, or belonging to the majority or minority?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, considering the circumstances and the civil war that was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: My second question is: Are you still a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And before, were you a member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was never involved in that. I was not a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Taya, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't have any questions either, which means that your testimony ends here, Mr. Dejanovic, and you're free to go back home. You will be escorted by Madam Usher, and you will receive all the assistance you need to make your trip back home possible. And on behalf of the Trial Chamber and on behalf of the Tribunal itself, I should like to thank you for having come over to give evidence, and we all wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So next week, we start on Monday, we're sitting in the morning. We have three sittings -- we have four sittings next week. You still have to confirm to me, Madam Registrar, what the situation for the 11th. Because yesterday I think it was tricky. We didn't have...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We already reserved a courtroom, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the 11th in the morning. We are sitting four days, Monday through Thursday, always in the morning. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the next witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before you move on, can we -- we are under the impression that we are doing one of these turn and turnabout weeks, that it was Monday in the mornings, Tuesday and Wednesday in the afternoons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, but not next week. That is the week after.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The week after, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The next witness is the one with the protective measures, correct, Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he is scheduled to last a day and a half?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: He is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the other three witnesses, you still intend to bring over in the course of next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That's my understanding at this point, Your Honour. And I'll inform the Court and the Prosecution if there's any changes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To confirm, we're talking of number 63, 64, and 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think in respect of the protective measures, Your Honours decided to have a talk to him, and then decide whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At first, yes, but I think we've decided to adopt that formality practically with every witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, the Prosecution don't raise an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On our side, it's not because we anticipate any problems, but we want to make sure that what he may have told Mr. Cunningham is indeed a real concern. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it was Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just then briefly mention, I have discussed this with Mr. Cunningham, but we would now request that as they have had the meetings with all the witnesses that we receive now a full list of who's actually coming. I understand that even though they've already -- as they told us that four major witnesses won't be coming, there may still be other witnesses who remain on their list or who are not testifying. Your Honour, as important, as I say, because of the resources that are otherwise devoted to a fruitless task. And if possible, we would like the order, the rough order in which they're going to be coming, and before Christmas, before the break at the end of week after next. And secondly, the summaries really now should come as a package, the full summaries. At the moment we still don't know who the third witness is because there has been two conflicting descriptions given of where he's from and what he's supposed to be doing. So -- if I've already -- as I say, I've discussed it -- I'm only mentioning so it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I think Mr. Ackerman has talked to Ms. Korner about providing her with the witnesses and their names, and I think that they have reached an agreement on that, so I don't see that's a problem. I think the confusion about Witness 64 I can address after Court with you because I think it's clarified in the summaries that were sent over today. If it isn't I'll -- we can talk to that after Court. The final thing I'd like to say is on behalf of the Defence to thank the Chamber for allowing Mr. Pytlik to attend. He's from California, and generally they're not allowed in places like this, but we appreciate the fact that the Chamber made an exception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a pleasure. In fact, I think it's an opportunity we would give gladly without reservation because it's an education in itself, also to watch the way direct and cross are conducted in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PYTLIK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I wish you all a nice weekend, and we will reconvene Monday morning, 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 8th day of December, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 25
